chunks: And as for what al-Saffar narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Ali ibn Sulayman from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Khattab, that he wrote to him asking about a cousin of his who had a slave girl serving him, and he would have intercourse with her. One day he entered her house and found a man serving her having intercourse with her, so he doubted about her [whether the child would be his or the servant's], so he threatened the slave girl, and she confessed that the man had committed fornication with her. Then she became pregnant and gave birth to a child.

So he wrote: If the child is yours or there is resemblance from you in him, do not sell them [the child and the mother], for that is not permissible for you. And if the son is not from you and there is no resemblance from you in him, then sell him and sell his mother, so that does not contradict what we have previously mentioned from the narrations.

Because the matter in that has been referred back to you, the owner of the slave girl, by considering [the signs of paternity]. If he knows that the child is from you by one of the means by which the attachment of children to fathers is established, he attaches him to you. And if the matter becomes ambiguous, he is prevented from selling him and does not attach him to you, according to what we have previously mentioned. And if he knows that he is not from you, it is permissible for him to sell him in all cases, according to what the news contained.

key_terms.فَجَرَ بِهَا: He committed fornication/sexual intercourse with her

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a slave girl and her child if she is impregnated by another man while owned by the first man?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Isfahani's chain in *al-Istibsar* clarifies the principle of *Ilqa'* (linking offspring to the father) in Shia jurisprudence, distinguishing between definitive paternity and mere resemblance. The Imam establishes that if the child is definitively his or shows clear resemblance, the owner retains the right to keep them but is prohibited from selling them, preserving the child's status; conversely, if paternity is excluded, the owner may sell both. This highlights the practical application of evidentiary standards in determining lineage and property rights within the slave system.
